record.paper_title: Open problems in PDE models for knowledge-based animal movement via nonlocal perception and cognitive mapping
record.original_question: How can one define measures of foraging success for cognitive movement models that account not only for overlap with resource density but also for the costs of foraging, such as metabolic expenditure or other energetic costs, so that success is measured as a result of successful foraging rather than only as correlation with where resources are located?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 44. How can we formulate different measures of foraging success that incorporate mechanisms beyond mere correlation with a resource density? More precisely, how can we meaningfully quantify costs (metabolic or otherwise) associated with foraging as a means to measure a species’ fitness as a result of successful foraging?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a cognitive animal movement model in which the population density u(x,t) of a foraging species on a spatial domain Ω ⊂ ℝ^n evolves according to a nonlocal/cognitive PDE of the general form

  ∂_t u = ∇·(D∇u − u A[u, R, m]) + f(u, R),

where R(x,t) ≥ 0 is a (possibly dynamic) resource density, m(x,t) is a cognitive map or memory variable encoding remembered resource locations, and A[u, R, m] is an advective drift built from nonlocal perception of R and m (so that individuals tend to move toward perceived high-resource regions).

A common, but coarse, scalar measure of foraging success is the resource-overlap functional

  F_overlap(t) = ∫_Ω u(x,t) R(x,t) dx,

which quantifies only the correlation between forager density and resource density.

Problem. Formulate alternative, biologically meaningful functionals F: (u, R, m, …) ↦ ℝ that quantify foraging success as a net outcome of foraging rather than as mere spatial correlation with R. Specifically, define a class of cost-aware foraging-success measures of the form

  F_net(t) = ∫_Ω G(u, R) dx  −  C[u, R, m](t),

where:

(i) G(u, R) represents resources actually acquired by foragers per unit time (e.g. a Holling-type functional response such as G(u,R) = u·h(R) with h saturating);

(ii) C[u, R, m] is a cost functional aggregating energetic expenditures associated with movement and cognition, for example of the form

  C[u, R, m](t) = ∫_Ω [ c_1 |v[u,R,m]|^2 u + c_2 |∇u|^2 / u + c_3 Φ(m) ] dx,

with v[u,R,m] the effective velocity field induced by A, the first term modeling metabolic cost of directed movement, the second a diffusive/exploratory cost, and Φ(m) a cost associated with maintaining and updating the cognitive map;

(iii) F_net should reduce, in appropriate limits (no movement cost, no cognition), to standard fitness proxies, and should admit comparison of different cognitive strategies (memory length, perception radius, learning rate) on the same model.

Provide (a) a precise definition of such cost-aware measures, (b) conditions on G, C, and on the PDE system ensuring that F_net is well-defined and finite for global-in-time solutions, and (c) a framework in which evolutionarily stable cognitive strategies can be characterized as maximizers of the long-time average

  lim sup_{T→∞} (1/T) ∫_0^T F_net(t) dt

over admissible parameters of the perception kernel and memory dynamics.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is posed as a modeling/open question concerning the design of cost-aware foraging-success functionals for cognitive movement PDEs. No published resolution providing a generally accepted definition has been identified; related work on cognitive/nonlocal movement PDEs continues to use resource-overlap or pure fitness proxies rather than energy-cost-adjusted functionals, suggesting the problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: Open problems in PDE models for knowledge-based animal movement
status_evidence.snippet: Survey lists open problems on cognitive movement PDEs, including how to quantify foraging success beyond resource correlation by incorporating metabolic and other costs.
status_evidence.claim: The question is stated as an unresolved open problem in a recent survey of PDE models for cognitive animal movement.
